problem:
Consider the vector subspace $H=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}.$ Which of the following vectors belong to ${H}^{⊥}?$

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -5 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider the vector subspace $H=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}.$ Which of the following vectors belong to ${H}^{⊥}?$

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as ${h}_{1}$ and ${h}_{2}.$ 

Now, a vector $v$ belongs to ${H}^{⊥}$ if $v$ is orthogonal to the set of vectors that spans the subspace $H.$ So, we have to find the products ${v}_{i}\cdot {h}_{j}$ for $i=1,2,3$ and  $j=1,2.$  

- For ${v}_{1}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {h}_{1} & =1\cdot (-2)+(-2)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot (-2)=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {h}_{2} & =1\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot 3+1\cdot 3=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{1}\in {H}^{⊥}.$

- For ${v}_{2}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\cdot {h}_{1} & =1\cdot (-2)+3\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot (-2)=-6\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{2}\notin {H}^{⊥}.$ We do not need to test ${v}_{2}\cdot {h}_{2}.$

- For ${v}_{3}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3}\cdot {h}_{1} & =3\cdot (-2)+(-6)\cdot (-2)+3\cdot (-2)=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {h}_{2} & =3\cdot 3+(-6)\cdot 3+3\cdot 3=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{3}\in {H}^{⊥}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{3}$ only".
